pending_articles.title: Dissociable episodic memory performance and subjective experience across the aphantasia imagery spectrum
pending_articles.content: Mental imagery is often assumed to support episodic memory, yet whether this relationship depends on conscious access to imagery, and how reduced imagery differs from total aphantasia, remains unclear. The present study compared objective episodic memory performance, subjective trial-by-trial vividness, confidence, and response times in people reporting normal imagery, reduced imagery, or total aphantasia, across younger and older age groups. Participants completed an incidental-encoding episodic memory task requiring identification of visual or spatial changes in targets within scenes, alongside trial-by-trial vividness and confidence ratings. Across the full imagery spectrum, trial-level fluctuations in vividness were related to memory performance, whereas trait-level and averaged vividness measures were not. Moreover, reduced imagery and total aphantasia showed dissociable patterns of episodic memory performance and subjective experience. In the reduced-imagery group, vividness was a stronger predictor of accuracy and response times, vividness judgements were slower, and confidence was lower, suggesting greater metacognitive uncertainty when imagery is weak and inconsistent. Controls outperformed reduced and aphantasic groups on visual but not spatial changes, and both groups responded more slowly than controls; confidence did not differ between control and aphantasic groups. Age-related memory decline was observed in the control and reduced groups but not in the aphantasic group. Exit questionnaire data highlighted limited awareness of aphantasia among typical imagers and a persistent belief among aphantasic participants that their memory was inferior. Together, these findings show that reduced imagery should be distinguished from total aphantasia rather than treating both as a single population, and that trial-level fluctuations in vividness reveal relationships with episodic memory that trait-level and averaged measures do not capture.

pending_articles.title: Daylight exposure improves sleep and subsequent sleepiness
pending_articles.content: Study Objectives: The causal effects of daylight exposure on sleep remain poorly understood, particularly under real-world conditions. This study aimed to address this gap by examining the effects of an afternoon daylight intervention on subsequent sleep. Methods: Ten healthy participants (4 males; 19 to 28 years) completed two randomized 3-h afternoon outdoor walks under high-intensity light (HIL; clear goggles) or attenuated light (AL; neutral-density-filtered goggles; ~10 photopic lux) conditions. Light exposure was centered around the estimated crossover between the phase-advancing and phase-delaying portions of the light phase-response curve, individually determined from baseline dim light melatonin onset (DLMO). Subsequent nocturnal sleep was assessed using at-home polysomnography (PSG), and subjective sleepiness and sleep quality were assessed using the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale and Groningen Sleep Quality Scale, respectively. Differences between conditions and across time were examined using linear mixed-effects models. Results: There were no significant differences between conditions in DLMO timing or the phase angle between DLMO and sleep onset, indicating that the light manipulation did not produce a detectable shift in circadian phase. Sleep duration and self-reported sleep quality were also unchanged. However, nighttime delta power accumulated more rapidly following HIL exposure, accompanied by greater NREM sleep and reduced wakefulness after sleep onset (all p < 0.01). Participants were also significantly less sleepy upon awakening following HIL compared with AL exposure (p < 0.05). Conclusions: High-intensity natural daylight exposure may promote greater sleep intensity and reduce sleepiness upon awakening. These findings highlight a potential role for daytime light exposure in modulating subsequent sleep physiology and next-morning sleepiness, independent of changes in circadian phase.

pending_articles.title: A vagal-to-sympathetic reflex controls lung vascular leak
pending_articles.content: Dynamic regulation of the vascular barrier is required for an effective inflammatory response, allowing delivery of plasma proteins and immune cells to sites of insult. Although normally protective, sustained leak becomes costly in organs like the lung, where swelling stiffens tissue and impairs breathing, yet many upstream regulators remain unidentified. Using a chemogenetic screen of vagal afferent subtypes, we identify a neural reflex that drives lung vascular leak. The reflex originates in an orphan population of neurons expressing Cysltr2 that innervates alveolar capillary beds and senses both mechanical and inflammatory stimuli, fitting classic definitions of pulmonary 'J' receptors, an afferent subtype described anatomically since the 1950s whose function has remained speculative. Activating CYSLTR2 neurons increases lung vascular leak within minutes and causes perivascular edema and respiratory dysfunction, whereas silencing them during inhaled allergen challenge reduces leak and improves lung mechanics. Rather than acting locally through antidromic peptide release, this reflex engages brainstem relays and sympathetic efferents to broadcast its effects throughout lung vasculature. Vagal control of the vascular barrier thus forms an axis of organ defense that can go awry in disease, revealing new ways to regulate organ fluid balance upstream of the endothelium

pending_articles.title: Lateral-eyed tree shrews combine panoramic vision with an expanded oculomotor repertoire
pending_articles.content: Mammals differ in how they redirect gaze. Primates shift and hold gaze with rapid, precise eye movements that can be decoupled from the head. In lateral-eyed mammals studied to date, gaze is organized around the head: saccades are coupled to head rotation in freely moving animals and typically accompanied by attempted head movements even under head fixation. These observations suggest a trade-off: animals that keep a panoramic field give up the precise, eye-driven control of gaze typical of frontal-eyed animals. But because lateral eyes and head-centered gaze co-occur in every lateral-eyed species studied, it is unknown whether one follows from the other. Here we test this in the tree shrew, an arboreal mammal with laterally placed eyes. Using real-time eye tracking in head-fixed animals, we find that tree shrews saccade frequently under head fixation and that most saccades occur without detectable attempted head movement. Tree shrews make visually evoked saccades, along both the horizontal and vertical axes of the visual field, toward targets. They can also fixate on visual targets. Using widefield calcium imaging, we show that visual cortex over-represents the central visual field. Lastly, we show that extraocular muscles contain morphologically elaborate palisade endings, specialized nerve endings that are a constant feature of frontal-eyed species. Lateral eyes therefore do not preclude eye-driven gaze control. The two are separable dimensions of visual system design, a combination that may suit animals whose locomotion routinely points the head away from where they need to look.

recently_processed.title: New software package: ERPLAB Studio
recently_processed.content:
We are excited to announce the release of a new EEG/ERP analysis package, ERPLAB Studio. We think it’s a huge improvement over the classic EEGLAB user interface. See our cheesy “advertisement” video to get a quick overview.

Rather than operating as an EEGLAB plugin, ERPLAB Studio is a standalone Matlab program that provides a more efficient and user-friendly interface to the most commonly used EEGLAB and ERPLAB routines.

With ERPLAB Studio, you automatically see the EEG or ERP waveforms as soon as you load a file. And as soon as you perform an operation, you see what the new EEG/ERP looks like. For example, when you filter the data, you immediately see the filtered waveforms.

You can even select multiple datasets and apply an operation like artifact detection on all of them in one step. And then you can immediately see the results, such as which EEG epochs have been marked with artifacts.

We give you access to EEGLAB’s ICA-based artifact correction tools, but with a nice bonus. You can plot the ICA activations in the same window with the EEG data, making it easy to see which ICA components correspond to specific artifacts such as eyeblinks.

The program has an EEG tab for processing continuous and epoched EEG data, and an ERP tab for processing averaged ERPs.

The automatic ERP plotting makes it easy for you to view the data laid out according to the electrode locations. And we have an Advanced Waveform Viewer that can make publication-quality plots.

ERPLAB Studio is mainly just a new user interface. Under the hood, we’re running the same EEGLAB and ERPLAB routines you’ve always used. And scripting is identical.

ERPLAB Studio is included in version 11 and higher of ERPLAB. You simply follow our download/installation instructions and then type estudio from the Matlab command line.

If you’re new to ERPLAB, we strongly recommend that you go through our tutorial before starting to process your own data.

If you already know how to use the original version of ERPLAB (which we now call ERPLAB Classic), you can quickly learn how to use ERPLAB Studio with our Transition Guide.

We also have a manual that describes every feature in detail.

recently_processed.title: Brain Age Gap Associations with Externalising Behaviours in Youth: A Longitudinal Investigation in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Cohort
recently_processed.content: Background. Early adolescence is a period of heightened risk for the emergence of externalising psychopathology, making it an important window for identifying neurodevelopmental risk markers. Differences between predicted brain age and chronological age - termed the brain age gap - reflect variation from age-typical patterns of brain structure. While brain age gap has been closely linked with internalising behaviours in adolescence, less is known about its relationship with externalising symptoms. This study examined whether brain age gap in late childhood/early adolescence (9-11 years) is associated with current externalising symptoms and whether it predicts externalising trajectories over seven-year follow-up. Methods. Participants were 10,516 adolescents (aged 9-11 at baseline; up to 18 years at follow-up) from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study who met inclusion/exclusion criteria. Brain age gap for each participant was derived from an external validated prediction model (Drobinin et al., 2022) applied to baseline measurements of cortical volume, area, and subcortical volume. Linear mixed-effects models were used to test cross-sectional and longitudinal associations between baseline brain age gap and externalising symptoms, as assessed using the Child Behaviour Checklist. Primary models were adjusted for age, sex, pubertal status, and prior to inclusion of sociodemographic covariates (ethnoracial identity and caregiver highest education). Results. A higher/more positive brain age gap was associated with greater externalising symptoms at baseline (B[SE]=0.067[0.033], p=.042), but this association was removed following sociodemographic adjustment (B[SE]=0.056[0.033], p=.088). Longitudinally, a significant brain age gap x age interaction was identified that remained evident after sociodemographic adjustment, with this relationship weakening across adolescence (B[SE]=-0.007[0.003], p=.033). Conclusions. These findings suggest that a more positive brain age gap, indicating more mature-appearing brain structure for age, in late childhood/early adolescence may be associated with externalising psychopathology, but this relationship is likely to be age- and context-dependent rather than a stable marker of persistent behavioural risk.

recently_processed.title: Scalable hardware and software for high-density, multi-regional electrophysiology in non-human primates
recently_processed.content: Understanding how distributed neural circuits generate complex behaviors requires long-duration recordings from populations of individual neurons across multiple brain regions. High-density Neuropixels probes have revolutionized rodent systems neuroscience. Extending these capabilities to non-human primates (NHPs) for chronic, multi-regional recordings requires compact, implantable microdrive hardware and reliable automated spike-sorting software. NHPs provide access to complex and flexible behaviors that are difficult to study in other model systems. Extending the Neuropixels revolution to NHPs therefore depends on integrating hardware and software for long-duration, multi-regional recordings. Here, we present a scalable hardware-software platform co-designed for high-density neural data acquisition and reliable single-unit identification in NHPs. The Multi-regional Implantable NeuroDrive (MIND) is a lightweight, implantable microdrive that provides stable recordings from multiple independently positioned Neuropixels probes and is designed to support chronic, ambulatory, head-free recordings. We paired MIND with UnitAssay, an automated post-sorting curation framework that identifies and curates characteristic spike-sorting errors with minimal computational cost. Together, MIND and UnitAssay provide an integrated platform for implanted, multi-regional recordings in NHPs performing complex and naturalistic behaviors. We tested MIND and UnitAssay across parietal, prefrontal, and motor cortices in rhesus macaques performing reaching and eye-movement tasks. MIND enabled stable multi-probe recordings across cortical regions and durations. UnitAssay enabled automated curation of large-scale spike-sorting output and improved reliable single-unit identification relative to Kilosort 4 labels and standard SpikeInterface quality control. Together, MIND and UnitAssay provide a scalable solution for high-density, multi-regional, long-duration electrophysiology in NHPs.

recently_processed.title: Enhancing working memories using repetitive TMS
recently_processed.content: Working memory, the ability to retain and manipulate information no longer present in the environment, is fundamental for goal-directed behavior (Baddeley, 2012; Baddeley & Hitch, 1974; D'Esposito, 2007; D'Esposito & Postle, 2015). Alpha oscillations (~8-12 Hz) have two apparently contradictory roles in working memory. Alpha activity gates irrelevant information through inhibition, a role causally supported by rhythmic transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of parietal cortex at alpha frequency when a retrospective cue renders a memory item irrelevant (Bonnefond & Jensen, 2012; Riddle et al., 2020). Yet alpha activity also tracks the content of memory and binds the features of memorized objects during maintenance (Foster et al., 2016; Pagnotta et al., 2026). Whether alpha oscillations causally support the fidelity of memory representations during maintenance is untested. Here, 24 participants received short trains of repetitive TMS (rTMS) at theta (6 Hz) or alpha frequency (10 Hz), or in an arrhythmic control pattern, during the second half of the delay of a color working memory task, over the left posterior inferior frontal sulcus or the left intraparietal sulcus. A mixture model separated memory precision from swap errors and guesses. Alpha stimulation of the intraparietal sulcus specifically increased memory precision, whereas rhythmic stimulation of either site reduced response error, guesses and swaps irrespective of frequency. These results provide causal evidence that alpha oscillations support the fidelity of working memory representations during maintenance, and show that rhythmic stimulation at the appropriate frequency, site and time can enhance human working memory.
recently_processed.author: Pagnotta, M. F., D'Esposito, M.

recently_processed.title: Manifolds for the neural representation of 3D spatial experience
recently_processed.content: The precision with which animals navigate and interact with objects depends in part on how their brains represent position and orientation in three dimensions. A central challenge is to explain within a common framework how neural systems ranging from insects to primates represent three-dimensional (3D) pose. Here we develop a framework based on the hypothesis that neural representations of pose lie on manifolds derived from the Special Euclidean Group, SE(3), which describes the full space of rigid-body positions and orientations in three dimensions. The framework shows how movement constraints, object geometry, and visual features jointly determine the topology of the resulting pose manifold, yielding a taxonomy that guides experimental tests. We apply the framework to derive low-dimensional manifolds for neural representations of 3D object orientation in macaque parietal cortex and head direction in the limbic systems of fruit bats, mice, and monkeys. This analysis also guides the construction of neuronal tuning functions that respect the topology determined by experimental conditions. Together, these results provide a common approach for linking the geometry of 3D pose to neural coding across species and brain systems.

recently_processed.title: Neurotransmitter receptor architecture links local neurochemistry to semantic memory
recently_processed.content: A fundamental challenge in neuroscience is understanding how the molecular and neurochemical architecture of the human cortex gives rise to sophisticated higher cognitive functions. The anterior temporal lobe (ATL) is a key hub for semantic memory, and its underlying GABAergic and glutamatergic neurochemistry supports semantic memory performance. However, the molecular receptor architecture underlying these neurochemical-cognitive relationships remains unknown. Here, we combined imaging transcriptomics and in vivo magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) to investigate how neurotransmitter receptor organisation relates to local neurochemistry and semantic memory in the human ATL. We found that the ATL exhibited a distinct transcriptomically inferred receptor-subunit profile relative to control cortical regions (occipital cortex and vertex). Individual-specific spatial estimates of receptor-subunit gene expression were systematically associated with local GABA+ and Glx concentrations, revealing preferential coupling between GABAergic receptor genes and GABA+ and between glutamatergic receptor genes and Glx, alongside widespread cross-system associations between GABAergic receptor architecture and Glx. ATL GABA+ and Glx concentrations were positively associated with semantic memory performance, and GABAergic and glutamatergic receptor-subunit expression showed selective relationships with semantic memory accuracy. Crucially, mediation analyses revealed that GABA+ mediated associations between GABAergic receptor architecture and semantic performance, whereas Glx mediated both glutamatergic and widespread GABAergic receptor associations. Together, these findings reveal a coupled molecular-neurochemical architecture of the human ATL, linking neurotransmitter receptor organisation to regional neurochemical state and individual differences in semantic memory. Our findings provide a multiscale account of how cortical molecular organisation is associated with human higher cognitive function.
recently_processed.author: Jung, J., Gim, J.-A., Lambon Ralph, M.

recently_processed.title: Heterogeneous plasticity rules generate diverse structures in recurrent networks
recently_processed.content: How do local changes at individual synapses give rise to structured recurrent connectivity? Experiments have revealed diverse forms of spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) across the brain, making it difficult to predict which circuit structures different rules will generate. We developed an analytical framework mapping excitatory Hebbian, anti-Hebbian, and symmetric STDP rules to directed three-neuron motifs. Individual homogeneous rules generate restricted subsets of motifs, and no single rule produces all motifs. Combining different rules generates motifs inaccessible to individual rules and yields the full motif repertoire, and these predictions generalize to larger recurrent networks. The mapping is nevertheless highly non-unique, with distinct rules and parameters producing similar motif distributions, including distributions compatible with experimental connectivity. Thus, circuit structure constrains candidate plasticity rules but does not uniquely identify them. Finally, networks with similar motif distributions can nonetheless differ in their firing rates and pairwise correlations, suggesting that activity may provide an additional constraint on candidate plasticity rules.
recently_processed.author: Cusseddu, C., Festa, D., Miehl, C., Gjorgjieva, J.

recently_processed.title: Cerebello-basal ganglia networks and behavior across adulthood and aging
recently_processed.content: The cerebellum contributes to aging, cognition, and reward related processing, but has been relatively understudied in these domains. The cerebello-basal ganglia (CB-BG) circuit may be key to better understanding how the brain ages. Prior work has implicated this circuit in aging in a small sample, though it is also of interest in age-related neurodegenerative disease, particularly Parkinson's Disease. Here, we investigated the CB-BG network, which has been implicated in modulation of cognitive, motor, and reward-related functions. In a sample of 138 participants between the ages of 35 and 86 we looked at network connectivity in cognitive and motor sub-circuits. Participants completed motor and cognitive testing batteries followed by 26 minutes of resting state functional connectivity magnetic resonance imaging (fcMRI). This data was analyzed using the CONN toolbox with an ROI-ROI approach targeting the CB-BG circuit. We replicated the previously mapped cognitive subcircuit and motor subcircuits. When examining connectivity by age group (early and late middle age and older adult hood), we found higher functional connectivity in early middle age compared to older adulthood, with no results related to late middle age. Analysis of connectivity as it relates to performance on the Stroop task showed higher connectivity-behavior associations in early middle-aged adults compared to older adults. We also explored sex differences and found higher functional connectivity in females compared to males. Analysis of steroid hormone levels revealed higher connectivity associated with progesterone in females relative to males. Together, we have replicated motor and cognitive CB-BG subcircuits and further demonstrated that this network has altered connectivity associated with age, sex, progesterone, and cognitive performance. This expanded investigation of CB-BG networks represents an essential new step in increasing our knowledge of age-related cognitive and motor declines and may be particularly relevant for consideration in Parkinson's Disease.
recently_processed.author: Delaney, C., Herrejon, I., Magalhaes, T. N. C., Jackson, T. B., Hicks, T. H., Bernard, J. A.

recently_processed.title: Ms4a4a loss preferentially remodels microglia with limited, compartment-specific effects across central and peripheral immune compartments in 5xFAD mice
recently_processed.content: Background: Genome-wide association studies have identified the MS4A locus as a major modifier of Alzheimers disease (AD) risk and resilience. MS4A4A is enriched in microglia, and we previously demonstrated that loss of Ms4a4a reduces amyloid plaque pathology and attenuates amyloid-associated tau spreading. However, MS4A4A is also expressed in peripheral myeloid populations, raising the possibility that its effects extend beyond brain-resident microglia. Here, we sought to define how constitutive Ms4a4a loss alters immune populations across central nervous system (CNS), CNS-border, and peripheral compartments in the context of amyloid pathology. Methods: We performed multicompartment immune profiling by flow cytometry in 5xFAD Ms4a4a wild-type and 5xFAD Ms4a4a-deficient mice. Myeloid and lymphoid populations were characterized in the brain, dural meninges, skull bone marrow, tibial bone marrow, and spleen. Results: Ms4a4a loss produced its strongest immune effects in brain microglia. 5xFAD Ms4a4a-deficient mice exhibited increased microglial abundance, increased frequency and expression of CD86, increased MHC class II expression intensity, and enrichment of CXCR4-high microglia, whereas P2RY12 and TREM2 were unchanged. Brain macrophages showed increased MHC class II expression, whereas conventional dendritic cells (cDCs) in the brain showed reduced MHC class II expression, with limited changes in other infiltrating immune populations. Immune composition in the dura and skull bone marrow was largely preserved, although MHC class II expression was increased in skull bone marrow cDCs. Peripheral immune composition in tibial bone marrow and spleen was similarly preserved, with selective increases in M2-like macrophages in tibial bone marrow and splenic CD8 T-cell frequency. Conclusions: These findings identify microglia as the immune population most strongly remodeled by Ms4a4a loss in the setting of amyloid pathology. Constitutive Ms4a4a deficiency does not produce broad systemic immune remodeling but instead preferentially alters microglial state, accompanied by more limited, cell type- and tissue-specific effects across other central and peripheral immune compartments. These findings establish MS4A4A as a context-dependent regulator of immune responses to AD pathology with particularly prominent effects on microglia.
